title: Agent Design Guidelines
about: The core file for the Agent Design Guidelines. The website, patterns.md and the Discovery Engine plugin all read from this file. Edit patterns here only. Pattern and principle ids never change; names, text and order can.

groups.name: Before the agent acts
groups.summary: Agree on what the agent may do, and when.

groups.name: While the agent acts
groups.summary: Show the work, and keep people in control of every decision.

groups.name: After the agent acts
groups.summary: Say honestly what happened, and keep a record anyone can follow.

groups.name: Over time
groups.summary: Let trust grow with a track record.

patterns.name: Agent disclosure
patterns.rule: Always clear what an agent did, from the very first interaction.
intro: We are required by law (AI Act, article 50) to clearly show when something is done by AI and agents. This needs to be done at the very first interaction, and not only in e.g. terms and conditions.
This can be done in many different ways depending on the context. Keep the marker consistent, and avoid human names and faces for agents.
look_for: A plain “Agent” label on every action
A marker that stays on each field it filled
A role name, never a person’s name or face
The same label in the log
patterns.do: The marker stays on the field, and the log says “Payroll agent”.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including suggestions, answers and work status.

items.what: Every proposal names the agent that made it, right next to the decision buttons. Try accepting or rejecting it.

items.marker: Drafted by agent, sent by you
items.what: Messages that reach clients say they were drafted by an agent, and which person sent them.
Ongoing work is listed per agent, with a spinner while it runs, so it is always clear what the agents are doing.

patterns.name: Autonomy levels
patterns.rule: A level per task, from Assistant to Autopilot, chosen by the person responsible.
intro: A named setting, such as Assistant, Copilot or Autopilot, chosen separately for each task, so low-risk work can run alone while high-risk work waits for approval.
look_for: The current level, visible per task
patterns.do: Reconciliation on Autopilot, payroll on Copilot, salary changes by a person only, each visible on screen.
patterns.avoid: One on/off switch for the whole product.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including levels per task, permissions per area and the level behind each action.

items.what: Each task has its own level, chosen by the person responsible. Change a level and see what the agent would do with the same work.
Within one agent, each area has its own permission. The agent acts where it is allowed, asks where it must, and stays out of the rest. Click a permission to change it.
Every action carries the level it ran at, so it is clear afterwards what the agent did alone and what a person approved.

patterns.name: Triggers
patterns.rule: Starts on its own when a date arrives or something happens, and says what started it.
intro: The agent starts on its own when a date arrives or something happens, such as a client replying, and reports what it did.
look_for: The trigger in words: “when time reporting closes”
What it did, reported where people already look
A way to pause the trigger
The next run date
patterns.do: It starts when time reporting closes, and says so: “Started on its own at 06:00.”
patterns.avoid: A “Run agent” button. Nothing happens until someone remembers.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including schedules, events and the start of a run.

items.what: Each trigger is written in plain words, with what it did last and when it runs next. A switch pauses a trigger without deleting it.
Scheduled agents sit next to the meetings they belong to. Agents that start on an event, like a new invoice, have no time slot, so they are listed beside the calendar.
When the agent starts on its own, the work opens with what started it and when, and ends with the next run date.

patterns.name: Suggestions
patterns.rule: Prepares the change and offers it as a button. Nothing happens before the tap.
intro: The agent prepares the change, or suggests the next step from what is in the books, and offers it as a button. It carries it out only when the person taps, instead of acting on their behalf unasked.
look_for: One clear confirm action
The offer says what it will do, and nothing happens until the tap
patterns.do: The agent prepares the change and offers it as a button. Nothing is sent until the person taps.
patterns.avoid: The agent acts first and tells you after.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including offers, a side-by-side comparison and next steps.

items.what: The offer says what will happen and who checks the result. Nothing is matched until the person taps.
The same change, offered as a button or made without asking. Switch between them to compare.
The agent suggests the next step where the work already is, with a preview of exactly what will be sent.

patterns.name: Live progress
patterns.rule: A count of the work and a running feed, with the rule behind each step.
intro: A progress indicator and running feed while the agent works, with the rule or confidence behind each step.
Announcing each step lets people who use a screen reader follow the run, pause it and take over.
look_for: A progress count: “48 of 64”
The rule or source behind each step
Named states: working, waiting, paused, done
A status message for every state change, and pause reachable by keyboard
patterns.do: “Collecting for 48 of 64 employees”, each finished check listed with the rule it used, and announced as “Step 3 of 5. Calculate depreciation. Agent working.”
patterns.avoid: A spinner, then a result. Or a bare 94%. Or progress shown only on screen.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including a running feed, sources for every claim and announced steps.

items.what: A count of the work, and a feed of finished checks, each with the rule or confidence behind it. Click a tag to see the reason.

items.marker: Every claim points to its source
items.what: Answers link each number to the document it came from. Click a source marker to see it.
Each step has a number and a named state. Every change is also sent to screen readers as a status message, and the run can be paused from the keyboard.

patterns.name: Failure disclosure
patterns.rule: What failed, why, what did not happen and what to do next.
intro: When the agent can’t finish, it says so plainly: what failed, why, what did not happen and what you can do next. It never covers a failure with a confident summary.
Record the outcome in the log, whichever way forward is chosen.
look_for: The failure named in the title, like “Bank file rejected”
The concrete cause, in the customer’s terms
What did not happen: “No payments were sent.”
A way forward: fix it, retry once, or hand it to a person
Empty results and low confidence said as such, not hidden
patterns.do: “Bank file rejected. The payment to Hamburg Stahl GmbH has no BIC code. No payments were sent.” Then: add the BIC and resend, send the other 2, or hand it to Anders.
patterns.avoid: “Something went wrong.” A failure styled like a normal result, or a run that keeps retrying forever.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including a rejected bank file, an empty search and a comparison with a cover-up.

items.what: The failure is named in the title, with the concrete cause and what did not happen, and the ways forward. The outcome is recorded either way.
When the agent finds nothing, it says so, and lists where it looked and where it couldn’t look.

items.marker: Not covered by a confident summary
items.what: The same failed payroll run, disclosed or covered up. Switch between them to compare.

patterns.name: Exceptions
patterns.rule: Routine work in one line. Only what needs judgement is listed, with the reason.
intro: Routine items are handled automatically and summarised in one line. Only the items that need judgement are listed, each with the reason it was flagged.
look_for: A count: “3 need you”
A card per item: problem, proposal, reason
Bulk actions only for the easy ones
An empty state when nothing needs you
patterns.do: One card per exception: the problem, the proposal and the reason.
patterns.avoid: Alerts for everything, and no proposal.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including a queue with reasons, bulk actions and an agent inbox.

items.what: Routine invoices are summed up in one line. The two that need judgement are listed with the reason they were flagged. Open one to see the problem, the proposal and the reason.

items.marker: Bulk actions only for the easy ones
items.what: Easy exceptions with the same fix can be handled together. The risky one, a new bank account, is left out of the bulk action and must be checked on its own.
Each agent posts what it needs from you, newest first, like email. The count goes down as you finish items, and an empty state says when nothing needs you.

patterns.name: Review and approve
patterns.rule: A before-and-after for every change, with accept, edit or reject.
intro: Each suggested change is shown as a before-and-after with its reason and three actions: accept, edit or reject. Taking over is always one tap away.
Show the reason and the rule with each change, and keep changes pending until a person saves. In our first sprint, “Accept all” hid what the agent changed.
look_for: Before and after, as a diff, with Accept, Edit and Reject
patterns.do: Accept or reject per change, with a diff on high-stakes fields.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including a diff with its reason, decisions per field and editing a draft.

items.marker: Before and after, with the reason
items.what: The change is shown as a diff, with the reason and the rule beside it. Accept, edit or reject it. Edit lets you pick another account before anything is booked.
Each field the agent wants to change gets its own decision, with high-stakes fields like the bank account marked. Nothing is saved until every change is decided and you press Save.
Taking over is one tap away. Edit the drafted reminder in place, go back to the agent draft, or send it as it is.

patterns.name: Clarifying questions
patterns.rule: One specific question with a best guess, instead of guessing.
intro: The agent recognises when it’s uncertain and asks a specific question instead of guessing or flagging the whole item. The question comes with its best guess, the alternatives and what it will do with your answer.
look_for: One specific question, about the part the agent doesn’t know
Its best guess, and why
The alternatives, each with what it will do
The rest of the work carrying on while the question waits
patterns.do: “Anna was off on Monday, but there’s no absence reason. Sick leave, vacation or unpaid leave? It affects her sick pay.” With sick leave marked as the best guess.
patterns.avoid: Booking unpaid leave straight away, or flagging the whole payslip for review.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including a question with a best guess, a question that doesn’t hold up the rest and a comparison with guessing.

items.marker: One question, with a best guess
items.what: The agent asks about the one thing it doesn’t know, leads with its best guess and why, and shows what each answer will do before you choose.

items.marker: Ask about the part, not the whole
items.what: Payroll keeps running for everyone else while one question waits. Answer it, and the last payslip is finished.
The same missing absence reason, asked about or guessed. Switch between them to compare.

patterns.name: Escalation
patterns.rule: Stops at the edge of the rules and hands the case to a named person.
intro: When the agent reaches the edge of the rules, or something fails, it prepares what it can, stops, and hands the case to a named person with what it checked, what failed and why it’s theirs.
Show the edge of the rules that started the escalation. For judgement calls, such as asset or repair, the case goes to the accountant.
look_for: A named person, not a queue, with what was checked and why it’s theirs
patterns.do: The excavator case handed to Anders with what was checked.
patterns.avoid: The case lands in a suspense account, or the agent guesses.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including a hand-over with context, a failure with ways forward and a comparison with a suspense account.

items.what: The agent prepares the case, stops, and hands it to Anders with what it checked and why it is his call. Open what was checked, or take the case.
When the agent can’t read the attachment, it says what failed and offers the ways forward: enter it yourself, ask a colleague or upload a readable copy.

items.marker: An owner, not a suspense account
items.what: The same case, handed to a person or parked in a suspense account. Switch between them to compare.

patterns.name: Undo
patterns.rule: Undo right where the result shows up, and a warning before what can’t be undone.
intro: Anything the agent did can be reversed right where it shows up, for as long as that is still possible, and the agent says before it acts what can’t be undone. An undo is logged like the action.
Payments, for example, can’t be undone once they leave the bank, so the agent says so before they go.
look_for: Undo where the result shows up, and how long it’s possible
What can’t be undone, said before it acts

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including undo on the result, a warning before what can’t be undone and a log of changes.

items.what: The undo sits on the reminder itself, with how long it is still possible. The undo is logged like the send.

items.marker: Says first what can’t be undone
items.what: Before the payments go, the agent says what can’t be reversed and until when they can still be stopped.

items.marker: The undo is logged, like the action
items.what: Every change has its undo where it is listed. A reminder is held for a few seconds before it sends, what can’t be unsent offers a correction instead, and each undo becomes a row of its own.

patterns.name: Audit trail
patterns.rule: A plain-language record of every run: what was read, changed and reviewed.
intro: A time-stamped record of every run: what the agent read, what it changed, which rules it used and who reviewed the result.
It should be a log an auditor or the tax authority could follow.
look_for: A timeline of steps
Who did each step: agent or person
Entries written as plain sentences
Undo from the log
patterns.do: Plain sentences, who approved what, and undo from the log.
patterns.avoid: Raw system logs, and no undo.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including a run step by step, a shared timeline with undo and a comparison with a raw log.

items.what: Each run is logged step by step: what the agent read, what it changed, which rules it used and who reviewed the result. Click an entry to see the details.
Agent steps and your own steps sit in one timeline, newest at the bottom. Your own actions carry your initials. Filter by who did it, and undo straight from the log.
The same three steps written for people, or as a raw system log. Switch between them to compare.

patterns.name: Recap
patterns.rule: A short summary with real numbers, and a brief when you come back.
intro: A regular summary with concrete numbers, such as time saved, issues caught and items handled without edits. When someone comes back to a long-running job, the agent first tells them what happened while they were away and what needs them now.
look_for: What it handled without asking, and what it caught
Your decision time, and where it was weaker
What needs you now, first
The details, one click later
patterns.do: How much was accepted without checking, how long decisions took, and what was caught. “Since Friday, 38 of 41 clients reconciled on their own. 3 need you.”
patterns.avoid: A count of messages sent. A list of every notification since Friday.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including a weekly recap, a thread summary and a brief when you come back.

items.what: A weekly card with concrete numbers: time saved, issues caught and how much was accepted without edits, and where the agent was weaker. Switch week, or click a number to see what is behind it.
A long thread opens with a short summary, and each point links to the message it came from. Click a number to see the message.
After a weekend away, the first thing you see is one line about what happened and what needs you. The details are one click away.

patterns.name: Earned autonomy
patterns.rule: Offers to do more after approvals without changes, and steps back after corrections.
intro: After several approvals without changes, the agent offers to do that action on its own. After corrections or reversals, it steps back and asks again.
Reminders, matching and coding can earn their way to Autopilot. Pay, filings and salary changes never do.
look_for: A track of approvals without changes
An offer to do more at a threshold
A step back after corrections
Things that never graduate: pay, filings, salary changes
patterns.do: After 10 approvals at 85% unchanged it offers more, and it steps back after two corrections.
patterns.avoid: It always asks, or it runs fully automatic from day one.

examples.intro: How the pattern can be applied in practice, including an offer at a threshold, a step back after corrections and levels that can be stepped through.

items.what: Each approval is tracked. After 10 approvals with at least 85% unchanged, the agent offers to send reminders on its own, and says how to switch it back.
When you correct the agent twice, it moves itself back a level and says why, and what it takes to earn the level again.
Everyone starts with no automation. Step up when the agent has earned it, or step down at any time. Pay, filings and salary changes never graduate.

principles.name: Lead with the work, not a prompt
principles.statement: The agent brings what needs attention. Nobody should have to know what to ask.

in_practice.text: The home screen is the recommendation. Most viewing starts there, not in search.
A new playlist for you every Monday. Nobody has to ask.
The tax return arrives pre-filled. If it’s right, you approve it by text message.
Nudges well ahead of VAT deadlines, and lists what still needs doing.

principles.name: The higher the stakes, the tighter the control
principles.statement: Routine work runs alone. Money, pay and filings wait for a person.

in_practice.text: Tap freely for small amounts. Above €50, or after a few taps in a row, the PIN is required.
You choose: always ask, ask before changes, or only before important changes. Bank transfers are refused.
Automatic reconciliation is switched on per bank account, and acts only when highly confident.
Copilot drafts the payment reminder; you stay in control of sending it.

principles.name: Never hide the agent, never hide the reason
principles.statement: Always labelled as an agent, and always showing why.

in_practice.text: Every message in spam says why it’s there.
On longer tasks, you can follow its progress step by step as it works.
Each auto-reconciled line says how: rule, match, memory or prediction.
A RULE badge shows when a bank rule categorised a transaction.

principles.name: Control is always one step away
principles.statement: Accept, edit, undo or take over, in one tap.

in_practice.text: Every email waits 5 seconds by default, up to 30, with Undo right there.
Interrupt, take over the browser, or stop the task at any point.
Change an account code or tax rate right on the Reconciled page, or remove and redo a match.

principles.name: Flag what’s new, not just what’s wrong
principles.statement: The unusual case is the one that matters.

in_practice.text: “You don’t often get email from…” appears when someone new writes.
“Be careful with this message” appears when a sender can’t be verified.
Adding a new payee triggers a name check, and shows the real name if it doesn’t match.
Checks your data and flags common mistakes HMRC would care about, before you file.
Bank transactions that match nothing are marked “Need your review” instead of being booked.

principles.name: Autonomy is earned, not granted
principles.statement: The agent proves itself run by run, and steps back when it’s wrong.

in_practice.text: Mark a message “Not spam” and the filter learns from it.
“Yes, don’t ask again” turns one approval into a standing permission for that action. Everything else still asks.
Bank rules suggest first. Booking automatically is a separate opt-in, per rule.
Off by default and switched on per account; “memory” decisions learn from how you reconciled before.

assessment.about: The "Assess your agent" page and its Claude review. One question per principle; each answer has three levels.

questions.question: How does work with the agent start?
answers: People type into a prompt box or chat
There’s a summary or suggestions, but chat is the main way in
The agent starts on its own at the right moment and brings what needs attention
questions.why: If people have to know what to ask, most of the agent’s value stays hidden.

fixes.title: Let the agent start the work
ideas: Start the agent on dates and events people already work to: time reporting closing, month-end, a client replying.
Open on a queue of what needs a person, each with the problem, the proposal and the reason.
Lead with a briefing: what happened and what needs you, before any list.

fixes.title: Make the queue the front door
ideas: Make the queue the default view, not a tab next to chat.
Say when the agent started on its own and why: “Started at 06:00, when time reporting closed.”
Show the next run date, and a way to pause the trigger.

questions.question: How is it decided what the agent may do on its own?
answers: Some actions need approval, but people can’t see which or why
A visible level per task: routine work runs alone; money, pay and filings wait for a person, and it stops at the edge of its rules
questions.why: When autonomy isn’t predictable, people either check everything or trust too much.

fixes.title: Set a level per task
ideas: Give each task its own level, such as Assistant, Copilot or Autopilot, so reconciliation can run alone while payroll waits for approval.
Keep bank payments, payroll and filings on approval only, with a named sign-off.
Show the current level on screen, next to the task.

fixes.title: Make each level visible, and offer before acting
ideas: Show the level on every task, and say why approval is needed.
For anything that leaves the company, let the agent prepare it and offer it as a button. Nothing is sent until the tap.
When a case falls outside the rules, stop and hand it to a named person instead of guessing.

questions.question: When the agent acts, what do people see?
answers: A one-time “AI” banner or a confidence score
A lasting “Agent” label on everything it did, the reason behind each step, and an honest account when something fails
questions.why: Without a label and a reason, people can’t tell what the agent did, so they check everything. Saying it’s AI is also a legal requirement in the EU.

fixes.title: Label the agent and show the reason
ideas: Put a plain role label, such as “Payroll agent”, on every action, on screen and in the log.
Show progress while it works: “48 of 64 employees”, each finished check with the rule it used.
Announce each step to screen readers: “Step 3 of 5. Calculate depreciation. Agent working.”

fixes.title: Replace banners and scores with labels and reasons
ideas: Replace one-time banners with a marker that stays on each field the agent filled.
Replace bare percentages with the rule or source behind each step.
When something fails, say what failed, why, what didn’t happen, and what to do next.

questions.question: Can people step in while and after the agent works?
answers: No: once it acts, it’s done
They can stop it, undo from a log, or correct it somewhere else
They can accept, edit or reject each proposal in one tap, undo right where the result shows, and take over a case at any point
questions.why: People trust an agent more when they know they can stop it, and know what can’t be reversed.

fixes.title: Add ways to step in
ideas: Show every proposal as a before-and-after, with Accept, Edit and Reject.
Add undo right where the result appears, with how long it’s still possible.
Say before acting what can’t be undone: “Payments can’t be undone once they leave the bank.”

fixes.title: Bring control to where the work is
ideas: Move undo out of the log and onto the result: “Sent 09:12. Undo for 10 minutes.”
Replace “Accept all” with a decision per change, and a diff on high-stakes fields such as a bank account.
Make correcting one action, in place, not a form somewhere else.

questions.question: What happens when something new or unusual comes in?
answers: It’s flagged only when an anomaly rule fires
New and unusual items go to an exceptions queue with the reason, and when it’s unsure it asks one specific question with a best guess
questions.why: Agents drift towards the familiar. In finance, the new supplier or the new rate is where the risk is.

fixes.title: Route the unusual to a person
ideas: Summarise routine work in one line, and list only the items that need judgement.
Give each exception one card: the problem, the proposal and the reason.
Show a count, “3 need you”, and an empty state when nothing does.

fixes.title: Raise what’s new, not just what’s wrong
ideas: Raise first occurrences too: a new supplier, a new VAT rate, a changed bank account.
When it’s unsure, ask one specific question with its best guess and one-tap answers, instead of guessing.
Check that flags don’t single out groups of employees, for example people on sick leave.

questions.question: How does the agent gain more autonomy over time?
answers: It’s fixed: it always asks, or it runs fully automatic from day one
Someone changes the setting by hand, with no track record to go on
It offers more after a track record of unchanged approvals, steps back after corrections, and pay and filings never graduate
questions.why: Autonomy granted all at once is either useless or reckless. A track record is what makes more autonomy safe.

fixes.title: Let autonomy be earned
ideas: Keep a plain-language activity log: who did what, which rules were used, and undo from the log.
Track approvals without changes, per task.
Start everyone at “it suggests, you choose”.

fixes.title: Base autonomy on the track record
ideas: Offer more at a threshold, such as 85% unchanged over 10 approvals, and let people say “Keep asking”.
Step back after two corrections, and say so.
Recap what was accepted without checking, decision time, what was caught and where it was weaker. Never graduate pay, filings or salary changes.

verdicts.name: An assistant bolted on
verdicts.meaning: Expect people to check everything the agent does, or not use it at all.

verdicts.name: Useful, not yet trusted
verdicts.meaning: People will use it, but most of its work will still be checked by hand.

verdicts.name: Trustworthy in parts
verdicts.meaning: Some workflows can run with a glance. Close the gaps before giving the agent more autonomy.

verdicts.name: Best-in-class
verdicts.meaning: On paper, this is ahead of every competitor we studied. Now prove it with measured acceptance.
